Empirical Research Plan: “Are housing‐supply constraints the reason Manhattan (and similar metros) are so expensive?”

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy:  Two–step IV difference-in-differences (a “Bartik-style interacted DID”).

•  First dimension (time): exogenous local demand shocks that vary year-to-year within each metro.  
•  Second dimension (cross-section): time-invariant “supply-constraint intensity” measured before our sample (1989 Wharton Land-Use index, zoning delays, % land landmarked, etc.).  

Main estimating equation  

Δln(Price_it) = β₁ DemandShock_it × SupplyConstraint_i + β₂ DemandShock_it  
                     + μ_i + λ_t + X_it γ + ε_it                        (1)

β₁ captures the extra price response to a demand shock in supply-constrained markets.  
Quantity regressions (permits or housing starts) give the mirror image.  

Endogeneity of DemandShock_it is handled with a Bartik instrument: National (outside-MSA) industry growth rates × 1980 metro industry mix.  
Because SupplyConstraint_i is predetermined (1989 survey), the interaction inherits the relevance & exogeneity of the Bartik shock (Goldsmith-Pinkham et al. 2023).  

Why appropriate?  
•  We can observe both prices and quantities over 1984-2002.  
•  Regulatory environment is largely fixed over this horizon.  
•  Exogenous labor-demand shocks split metros into “treated” (tight land-use) vs “control” (elastic) in exactly the way theory predicts: if high prices are due to supply constraints, shocks raise prices more and output less in constrained places.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable
  SupplyConstraint_i : continuous Wharton index (0=very lax … 1=very strict). In some robustness, define Treated = top quartile of the index.

Control group
  Bottom quartile metros (elastic supply such as Atlanta, Dallas, Kansas City).

Treatment timing / event
  No single event; instead we exploit annual demand shocks 1984-2002. Exposure varies continuously with the size of the Bartik shock. Conceptually each positive employment shock in year t is an “event” whose impact is contrasted across constrained vs unconstrained metros.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Exogeneity of the Bartik shock: National industry growth is orthogonal to unobservable, metro-specific supply factors after removing national time effects.  
Plausibility: Manhattan’s zoning board does not influence nationwide industry booms; we exclude the MSA itself from national growth (standard leave-one-out).  

A2. SupplyConstraint_i is predetermined and time-invariant over 1984-2002.  
Plausibility: Land-use regulations change only slowly; 1989 survey predates most of the price run-up we analyse.  

A3. In the absence of demand shocks, high- and low-constraint metros would have parallel price trends (conditional on controls and μ_i, λ_t).  
Plausibility check: pre-trend graphs and placebo leads (event-study style).  

A4. First-stage relevance: Bartik shock strongly predicts employment growth.  
Can be tested in data (F-stat > 10).  

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Remedies
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Endogenous regulation (cities raise zoning when prices rise).  
  •  Use regulation measured in 1989 (before much of the 1990s boom).  
  •  Show results robust to using physical/topographic supply-elasticity measures (Saiz 2010 land unavailability).  

T2. Bartik instrument violated by local industry shocks (e.g., finance centered in NYC).  
  •  Leave-one-industry-out robustness (exclude finance, high-tech).  
  •  Use alternative shocks: immigration flows driven by national origin quotas, defense procurement booms.  

T3. Differential unobserved amenities trending with regulation.  
  •  Include MSA-specific linear trends.  
  •  Control for crime, school quality, and climate interacted with year.  
  •  Event-study coefficients for leads should be flat if assumption holds.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ------------- 0. packages -------------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)       # fast TWFE & IV
library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)

# ------------- 1. load data -------------
price <- read_csv("condo_transactions_manhattan_1984_2002.csv")     # condo prices
ahs   <- read_csv("AHS_21_metros_1991_1999.csv")                    # owner-occ AHS
cost  <- read_csv("construction_cost_estimates.csv")                # Means, M&S
regs  <- read_csv("wharton_landuse_1989.csv")                       # supply constraint
perm  <- read_csv("census_building_permits_1955_2002.csv")          # quantities
labor <- read_csv("bea_employment_by_industry_msa.csv")             # local
nat   <- read_csv("bea_employment_by_industry_national.csv")        # national

# ------------- 2. variable construction -------------

# (a) Annual metro-level price per sqft (condos & AHS blended)
house_price <- price %>%
  mutate(year = lubridate::year(sale_date)) %>%
  group_by(msa, year) %>%
  summarise(p = median(price_2002usd_per_sqft)) %>%
  ungroup()

# (b) Construction cost (take flat real cost within metro-year)
cost_msa <- cost %>% select(msa, cost_2002usd_per_sqft)

# (c) Markup
house_price <- left_join(house_price, cost_msa, by = "msa") %>%
  mutate(markup = log(p) - log(cost_2002usd_per_sqft))

# (d) Supply-constraint index
house_price <- left_join(house_price, regs, by = "msa")  # variable: supply_idx (0-1)

# (e) Bartik demand shock
# Compute national growth by industry excluding the focal MSA
growth_nat <- nat %>%
  group_by(year, industry) %>%
  summarise(nat_growth = (employment - lag(employment))/lag(employment)) %>% ungroup()

growth_local <- labor %>%
  group_by(msa, industry) %>%
  mutate(lag_emp = lag(employment)) %>%
  ungroup()

bartik <- growth_local %>%
  left_join(growth_nat, by = c("industry", "year")) %>%
  group_by(msa, year) %>%
  summarise(bartik = sum(lag_emp * nat_growth, na.rm = TRUE)/sum(lag_emp, na.rm=TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup()

house_price <- left_join(house_price, bartik, by = c("msa", "year"))

# ------------- 3. main regression -------------
# TWFE IV: Δlog price on Bartik × supply_idx instrumented by same interaction with bartik_iv
panel <- house_price %>%
  group_by(msa) %>%
  arrange(year) %>%
  mutate(d_ln_price = log(p) - log(lag(p))) %>%
  mutate(d_bartik = bartik - lag(bartik)) %>%
  ungroup()

# Interaction and first stage
panel <- panel %>%
  mutate(interact   = d_bartik * supply_idx)

# Regression
est_price <- feols(d_ln_price ~ 1 | msa + year | interact ~ d_bartik,
                   data = panel, cluster = ~msa)

summary(est_price)

# Quantity response (permits)
permits <- perm %>%
  group_by(msa, year) %>%
  summarise(starts = sum(units)) %>% ungroup()

panel_q <- left_join(permits, bartik, by = c("msa","year")) %>%
  left_join(regs, by = "msa") %>%
  group_by(msa) %>%
  arrange(year) %>%
  mutate(d_ln_starts = log(starts) - log(lag(starts)),
         d_bartik    = bartik - lag(bartik),
         interact    = d_bartik * supply_idx) %>% ungroup()

est_qty <- feols(d_ln_starts ~ 1 | msa + year | interact ~ d_bartik,
                 data = panel_q, cluster = ~msa)

# ------------- 4. robustness: placebo leads -------------
panel <- panel %>%
  mutate(lead_bartik = lead(d_bartik, 2),
         lead_int    = lead_bartik * supply_idx)

placebo <- feols(d_ln_price ~ lead_int | msa + year, data = panel, cluster=~msa)
coeftest(placebo, vcov = vcovCL, cluster = ~msa)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory predicts β₁ > 0 in (1).  
Rough magnitude priors (per 1 ppt employment shock):

•  Constrained metros: +2.0 – 2.5 % increase in real prices.  
•  Unconstrained metros: +0.5 % (β₁ ≈ 0 when supply_idx = 0).  

Quantity mirror image: constrained metros show essentially zero or even negative permit response; elastic metros raise permits 1.5–2 %.  

Implied mark-up over construction cost remains ≥40 % in Manhattan versus ≈10 % in elastic heartland cities.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV-DID)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
C1 (Relevance: strong first stage) …………………… 1  
C2 (Exogeneity of instrument) ………………………… 0.5  
C3 (Parallel trends across constraint groups) …… 0.8  
C4 (Stable regulation over time) …………………… 0.9  
C5 (No spillovers across metros) …………………… 0.7  

Overall: method is credible but rests mainly on the exogeneity of labor-demand shocks and the assumption that regulation is predetermined.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
